abstract: When cultured in the presence of either retinoic acid (RA) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), aggregates of the P19 line of mouse embryonal carcinoma (EC) cells differentiate and the spectrum of cell types formed depends on the drug dose. It is shown here the EC cells rapidly lose their colony-forming ability when cultured as aggregates in the presence of DMSO. This loss of plating efficiency (PE) also occurs rapidly following RA treatment. Loss of PE has been used as a quantitative procedure for assessing the rate of drug-induced differentiation. The relationship between drug dose and loss of PE is much steeper for DMSO than for RA, suggesting that these two drugs affect different stages of the differentiation decision-making apparatus. Mutant EC cell lines (D3 and RAC65) do not differentiate in the presence of drug-inducers (DMSO and RA, respectively). Neither differentiation-deficient mutant has an altered ability to form gap junctions. When D3 and P19 cells were mixed within the same DMSO-treated aggregates, the D3 cells remained undifferentiated and the P19 cells differentiated much less efficiently than if they were cultured in the absence of the D3 cells. When RAC65 and P19 cells were mixed in RA-treated aggregates, each cell responded to the drug as though the other were absent. Thus RA behaves as a cell-autonomous inducer of differentiation, whereas DMSO-induced differentiation seems to be mediated by interactions between neighboring cells.
abstract_ja: P19マウス胎児性癌(EC)細胞の凝集体は、レチノイン酸(RA)またはジメチルスルホキシド(DMSO)存在下で培養すると分化し、形成される細胞種は薬剤の用量に依存する。本研究では、凝集体をDMSO存在下で培養するとEC細胞は急速に plating efficiency(PE)、すなわちコロニー形成能を失うことを示す。RA処理後にも急速なPEの低下が見られる。PEの低下は薬剤誘導分化の速度を定量する指標として用いられてきた。用量とPE低下の関係は、RAよりもDMSOの方が急峻であり、両薬剤が分化決定機構の異なる段階に作用することを示唆している。分化欠損変異株であるD3およびRAC65は、それぞれDMSOおよびRAという誘導剤に反応しない。いずれの分化欠損変異株もギャップ結合の形成能に変化はない。D3とP19細胞を同一のDMSO処理凝集体内で混合すると、D3細胞は未分化のままで、P19細胞はD3細胞が存在しない場合と比べて分化の効率が著しく低下した。RAC65とP19細胞をRA処理凝集体内で混合すると、各細胞はもう一方の細胞が存在しないかのように薬剤に応答した。したがって、RAは細胞自律的な分化誘導因子として作用するのに対し、DMSOによる分化誘導は隣接細胞間の相互作用によって媒介されると考えられる。
